In a metal the valence electrons are not tied to any one atom. They form a delocalised sea of
mobile electrons moving freely through a lattice of positive ions.
When light strikes the surface, these free electrons absorb the incident photons and are set
oscillating. Being mobile and unbound, they immediately re-emit radiation of the same
frequency back out of the surface.
That re-emission is what we see as the metallic lustre, and it is why a freshly cut metal
surface is so bright across the whole visible range.
The same free electrons account for the other metallic properties — electrical conductivity,
thermal conductivity and malleability.
(1) and (4) are irrelevant: dense and inert non-metals exist without lustre.
(2) is the wrong way round — polishing reveals the lustre, it does not cause it; the shine of a
polished non-metal is ordinary specular reflection, not this electronic effect.
∴ reflection of light by mobile electrons.

kcet|Chemistry|2013|50||0|0.s:
Elevation of boiling point is ΔTb = i·Kb·m, so the highest boiling point goes to the solution
with the largest number of dissolved particles — the largest i × concentration.
Work out i × C for each:
(1) 0.01 M urea — does not dissociate, i = 1 ⇒ 0.01
(2) 0.01 M KNO₃ — gives K⁺ + NO₃⁻, i = 2 ⇒ 0.02
(3) 0.01 M Na₂SO₄ — gives 2Na⁺ + SO₄²⁻, i = 3 ⇒ 0.03 ← largest
(4) 0.015 M glucose — does not dissociate, i = 1 ⇒ 0.015
Sodium sulphate wins because it yields three ions per formula unit, which more than makes up
for the higher concentration of the glucose solution.
Note that the identity of the solute is irrelevant beyond the particle count — that is what
makes this a colligative property.
∴ 0.01 M Na₂SO₄.

Spontaneity is decided by the sign of the Gibbs free energy change:
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS
A process is spontaneous when ΔG < 0.
Go through the four combinations.
(2) ΔH negative and ΔS positive — the first term is negative and −TΔS is also negative, so ΔG
is negative at **every** temperature. Spontaneous always ✓
(1) ΔH positive and ΔS negative — both terms positive, so ΔG is positive at every temperature.
Never spontaneous.
(3) ΔH positive and ΔS positive — the two oppose each other; spontaneous only at high enough
temperature, above T = ΔH/ΔS.
(4) ΔH positive and ΔS zero — ΔG = ΔH > 0, so never spontaneous.
So only one of the four guarantees spontaneity at the given temperature, whatever it is.
∴ ΔH is −ve and ΔS is +ve.

HI with red phosphorus is a powerful reducing combination. It replaces every –OH group of a
molecule by –H, and the red phosphorus regenerates the HI as it is consumed, so the reduction
goes right through to the hydrocarbon.
Glucose is CH₂OH–(CHOH)₄–CHO: a straight chain of **six** carbons.
Prolonged reduction strips off all five hydroxyls and reduces the aldehyde as well, leaving only
the carbon skeleton saturated with hydrogen:
C₆H₁₂O₆ + HI/red P ⇒ CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃
The carbon count is unchanged, so a six-carbon sugar gives a six-carbon alkane.
Historically this was an important experiment: it proved that glucose has an **unbranched**
chain of six carbons, since a branched skeleton would have given a branched hexane isomer.
∴ n-hexane.
kcet|Chemistry|2013|55||0|0:
A lyophobic sol — such as a metal sol or As₂S₃ — has no affinity for the dispersion medium,
so there is no solvation layer to hold it together. Left to itself it would coagulate at once.
What keeps it dispersed is **electrical charge**. Each colloidal particle preferentially adsorbs
one kind of ion from the medium, so every particle carries the same sign of charge. Like
charges repel, and that repulsion prevents the particles from approaching closely enough to
coalesce.
This is exactly why adding an electrolyte coagulates a lyophobic sol: the added ions neutralise
that charge, the repulsion vanishes, and the particles clump and settle. It is also why the
Hardy–Schulze rule works, the coagulating power rising steeply with the charge on the
oppositely charged ion.
(1) describes nothing real here, (2) size alone gives no stability, and (4) the Tyndall effect is
merely how a colloid is detected, not what stabilises it.
∴ the charge on the particles.

Oils and fats are both triesters of glycerol with long-chain fatty acids; what separates them is
the degree of unsaturation of those acid chains.
A **saturated** chain is straight, so the molecules pack closely, the van der Waals attraction
between them is large, and the melting point is high. Those are the fats — solid at room
temperature — and their salts are palmitates, stearates and myristates.
An **unsaturated** chain has a cis double bond, which puts a permanent kink in it. The kinked
chains cannot pack neatly, the attraction between them is weaker, and the melting point drops
below room temperature. That gives a liquid oil.
Oleic acid is the common unsaturated one, C₁₇H₃₃COOH with one C=C, so oils are rich in
**oleates**.
This also explains hydrogenation: adding H₂ across those double bonds straightens the chains
and turns a liquid oil into a solid fat, which is how vanaspati is made.
∴ oleates.
